_about: Curated library of proven traffic-safety countermeasures with cited crash-reduction effect sizes from peer programs and research. Referenced by data/recommendations.json so every recommendation names a mechanism and an evidence-backed effect rather than an opaque score.
_verification_note: Effect sizes are transcribed from the cited sources but have NOT each been re-verified against the primary document. Treat `effect_size` as research-grade until `verified` is true. Per the project editorial promise, re-check each figure before presenting it as settled fact.

countermeasures.name: Leading pedestrian interval (LPI)
countermeasures.mechanism: Gives people on foot a 3-7 second head start into the crosswalk before parallel traffic gets a green, so turning drivers see and yield to pedestrians already in the intersection.
countermeasures.effect_size: Seattle reported roughly -34% serious-injury/fatal pedestrian crashes and -48% pedestrian turning collisions at LPI locations.

countermeasures.name: Daylighting (clear-sight corners)
countermeasures.mechanism: Removes parking within ~20 feet of a crosswalk so drivers and pedestrians can see each other before the conflict point; often paired with bump-outs.
countermeasures.effect_size: Core to Hoboken NJ's multi-year stretch with zero traffic deaths, deployed at 130+ intersections alongside high-visibility crosswalks and curb extensions.
countermeasures.source_title: Results4America — Improving Traffic Safety in Hoboken, NJ

countermeasures.name: Road diet / lane rechannelization
countermeasures.mechanism: Converts a wide multi-lane road (e.g. 4 lanes to 3 with a center turn lane plus bike lanes), cutting speeding and turning conflicts and shortening pedestrian crossings.
countermeasures.effect_size: FHWA cites ~19-47% total crash reductions for road diets; Seattle's Nickerson St saw roughly -93% aggressive (top-end) speeding.
countermeasures.source_title: FHWA Vision Zero Toolkit; Seattle SDOT

countermeasures.name: Automated speed enforcement
countermeasures.mechanism: Cameras ticket speeding automatically, lowering top-end speeds where crash severity rises steeply with speed. Most effective when sited on the High Injury Network and paired with engineering.
countermeasures.effect_size: A DDOT study reported injury crashes falling from 841 to 673 (about -20% injuries) around enforced locations; Portland measured -71% to -93% top-end speeding within 30 days of activation.
countermeasures.equity_caution: Enforcement-heavy measures can fall unevenly; pair with engineering and review ticket distribution. Prefer engineering/speed-management fixes where they address the problem directly.
countermeasures.source_title: DDOT speed-camera study (TRB); Portland safety cameras

countermeasures.name: Curb extension / bump-out
countermeasures.mechanism: Extends the sidewalk at a crossing, shortening the pedestrian exposure distance, slowing turning vehicles, and improving sight lines.
countermeasures.effect_size: A standard component of low-cost Vision Zero packages (e.g. Hoboken's 60+ curb extensions) credited in its sustained zero-death record.

countermeasures.name: Protected intersection
countermeasures.mechanism: Corner islands, setback crossings, and dedicated signal phases physically separate people biking and walking from turning vehicles.
countermeasures.effect_size: Widely deployed in Vision Zero programs to remove turning conflicts at high-injury intersections; effect varies by site (verify locally).

countermeasures.name: 20 mph default speed limit
countermeasures.mechanism: Lowering speed limits (with supporting design) reduces both crash frequency and the probability that a struck pedestrian is killed, which rises sharply above 20-25 mph.
countermeasures.effect_size: Part of Hoboken's and London's Vision Zero approach; pedestrian survival probability is far higher in a 20 mph than a 30+ mph impact.
countermeasures.source_title: TfL Vision Zero for London; Hoboken
